questions.stem:
During a site visit to a parking structure, the architect sees the contractor's crew preparing to place concrete in a post-tensioned deck. The specified special inspection of the tendon layout hasn't been performed, and the contract requires it before placement. The superintendent says the inspector is running late and the trucks are already on site.

What should the architect do?

options.text: Order the contractor to stop all work on the site
options.explanation: The architect has no authority to stop the work. That right belongs to the owner.

options.text: Reject the work if placed, and notify both parties
options.explanation: Correct. The architect can reject nonconforming work and should notify the owner and contractor in writing. The owner can decide whether to stop the work.

options.text: Direct the concrete subcontractor to send the trucks away
options.explanation: The architect communicates with subcontractors through the contractor.

options.text: Wait for the inspector's report before taking any action
options.explanation: By then the concrete may be placed and the problem hidden.

questions.explanation: The architect rejects nonconforming work. The owner has the right to stop the work.
questions.confidenceNote: Paragraph number per my knowledge of the AIA document; confirm against your copy (free via your NCARB Record).

questions.stem:
An architect is reviewing the contractor's fifth application for payment on a school. The architect's site visit confirms the work and the stored materials, which are suitably stored and insured. The figures are:

- Work completed to date: $1,200,000
- Materials stored on site: $100,000
- Retainage: 10%
- Previous certificates: $900,000

What amount should the architect certify?

options.explanation: This leaves out the stored materials.
This takes retainage only on the stored materials.
This leaves out retainage.

questions.stem:
After the architect certified a progress payment on a medical office building, the owner learns that the contractor hasn't paid its drywall subcontractor, which has filed a lien. The owner says that by certifying the payment, the architect told the owner the subcontractors had been paid.

What does the architect's certificate for payment represent under A201-2017?

options.text: That the architect verified the subcontractors were paid
options.explanation: The certificate isn't a representation about how the contractor used the money.

options.text: That the work progressed as indicated, to its knowledge
options.explanation: Correct. The certificate reflects the architect's knowledge, information and belief from its site visits and the data in the application.

options.text: That the architect has made exhaustive inspections of the work
options.explanation: Site visits aren't exhaustive inspections.

options.text: That the completed work is free of all defects
options.explanation: The certificate doesn't guarantee the work.

questions.explanation: §9.4.2: the certificate states progress and quality to the architect's knowledge, not how the money was used.

questions.stem:
During construction of a fire station, the owner decides to add a backup generator. The contractor's price is $96,000, and the owner thinks it should be $70,000. The generator pad must be poured next week with the adjacent slab or the schedule will slip, so the owner wants the work to proceed while the price is negotiated.

Which document should the architect prepare?

options.text: A change order
options.explanation: A change order needs agreement on the price and time, which the parties don't have yet.

options.text: A construction change directive
options.explanation: Correct. A CCD, signed by the owner and architect, directs the change before the price is agreed.

options.text: An order for a minor change in the work
options.explanation: Minor changes can't change the contract sum.

options.text: Architect's supplemental instructions
options.explanation: ASIs clarify the documents but don't authorize a change in cost.

questions.explanation: Use a CCD when the work must proceed before the price is agreed.

questions.stem:
A contractor notifies the architect that a new library is substantially complete and submits its list of items to complete or correct. During the inspection, the architect finds the building usable for its intended purpose, but also finds several deficiencies that aren't on the contractor's list. These include damaged ceiling tiles and a missing door closer.

What should the architect do?

options.text: Reject substantial completion until every item is corrected
options.explanation: Substantial completion doesn't require every item to be finished, only that the building be usable.

options.text: Add the items to the list and prepare the certificate
options.explanation: Correct. Items the architect finds are added to the list, and the certificate of substantial completion is issued with the list attached.

options.text: Issue the certificate based only on the contractor's list
options.explanation: The architect adds the items its inspection finds.

options.text: Ask the owner to inspect and add any items it finds
options.explanation: The completion inspection is the architect's duty.

questions.explanation: §9.8: add the items found, then certify substantial completion with the list.

questions.stem:
The architect approved the storefront shop drawings for a retail building. After installation, the architect finds that the mullions are a different profile than specified. The shop drawings showed the different profile, but the contractor didn't call it out as a deviation. The contractor says the architect's approval accepted the change.

Who is responsible for the deviation?

options.text: The architect, because it approved the shop drawings
options.explanation: Approval doesn't accept a deviation that wasn't specifically identified.

options.text: The contractor, because it didn't identify the deviation
options.explanation: Correct. The contractor isn't relieved of a deviation unless it informed the architect in writing and the architect specifically approved it.

options.text: The storefront manufacturer, which prepared the drawings
options.explanation: The manufacturer works for the contractor, so the contractor remains responsible to the owner.

options.text: The owner, because its architect approved the submittal
options.explanation: The owner doesn't take on the contractor's responsibility through the architect's review.

questions.explanation: §3.12.8: unflagged deviations stay the contractor's responsibility.
questions.confidenceNote: Paragraph number per my knowledge of the AIA document; confirm against your copy (free via your NCARB Record).

questions.stem:
The owner and contractor of a university building disagree about whether the installed brick matches the approved sample panel. The contractor says the color range is acceptable. The owner wants a section removed and rebuilt. Both ask the architect for a decision, and the architect finds the installed brick consistent with the approved sample.

Which statement describes the architect's decision?

options.text: It's final, because it concerns aesthetic effect
options.explanation: Correct. Decisions on aesthetic effect are final if consistent with the intent of the contract documents (§4.2.13).

options.text: It's advisory until the owner accepts it in writing
options.explanation: Under A201, the architect's aesthetic decisions consistent with intent are final.

options.text: It must go to mediation before it takes effect
options.explanation: Aesthetic decisions consistent with intent don't go through the claims process.

options.text: It binds the contractor, but the owner may overrule it
options.explanation: The architect interprets impartially, and its decision binds both parties.

questions.explanation: Aesthetic decisions consistent with the documents' intent are final.
questions.confidenceNote: Paragraph number per my knowledge of the AIA document; confirm against your copy (free via your NCARB Record).

questions.stem:
The owner of a hospital expects the architect's construction administration to include checking every weld on the steel frame and being on site daily. The architect's agreement provides basic construction-phase services with site visits every two weeks, and the owner has engaged a testing agency for the welds.

How should the architect respond?

options.text: Agree to check every weld within basic services
options.explanation: Basic CA site visits are periodic, not exhaustive inspections.

options.text: Explain visits are periodic and offer on-site representation
options.explanation: Correct. Full-time on-site representation is a supplemental service. Weld inspection is the testing agency's job.

options.text: Have the contractor's quality-control staff report to the owner
options.explanation: The contractor's QC doesn't replace the architect's role or the owner's testing agency.

options.text: Refer the owner to the building inspector for daily visits
options.explanation: The building inspector enforces the code. It doesn't represent the owner.

questions.explanation: Site visits are periodic. Continuous on-site representation is a separate service.
questions.confidenceNote: Paragraph number per my knowledge of the AIA document; confirm against your copy (free via your NCARB Record).

questions.stem:
The contractor for a community center submits a claim for 15 additional days, saying the owner's late delivery of furniture blocked finish work. The owner disputes it. The owner–contractor agreement uses A201-2017 and doesn't name anyone other than the architect as Initial Decision Maker. The contractor asks what happens next.

How should the claim be handled first?

options.text: It goes directly to binding arbitration
options.explanation: Under A201-2017, an initial decision normally comes before mediation and binding resolution.

options.text: The architect renders an initial decision as IDM
options.explanation: Correct. The architect is the Initial Decision Maker unless someone else is named.

options.text: The owner decides it, as the party paying for time
options.explanation: The owner is a party to the dispute and doesn't decide claims.

options.text: It goes to mediation before anyone reviews it
options.explanation: Mediation follows the IDM's decision.

questions.explanation: A201 claims: IDM decision → mediation → binding resolution.
